{{Short description|Term in geometry and fractal analysis}}
{{Use American English|date = January 2019}}
[[File:Rotational Invariance Example.gif|thumb|right| Figure 1. Basic fractal patterns increasing in '''lacunarity''' from left to right.]]
[[File:Rotational Invariance rotated.gif|thumb|right| The same images as above, rotated 90°. Whereas the first two images appear essentially the same as they do above, the third looks different from its unrotated original. This feature is captured in measures of lacunarity listed across the top of the figures, as calculated using standard biological imaging box counting software {{harvnb|FracLac|loc=[https://web.archive.org/web/20000118104829/http://rsb.info.nih.gov/ij/plugins/index.html Image] }}.]]

'''Lacunarity''', from the Latin [[wikt:lacuna|lacuna]], meaning "gap" or "lake", is a specialized term in [[geometry]] referring to a measure of how patterns, especially [[fractal]]s, fill space, where patterns having more or larger gaps generally have higher lacunarity. Beyond being an intuitive measure of gappiness, lacunarity can quantify additional features of patterns such as "[[rotational invariance]]" and more generally, heterogeneity.<ref name="smith">{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Smith | first1 = T. G. 
| last2 = Lange | first2 = G. D. 
| last3 = Marks | first3 = W. B. 
| doi = 10.1016/S0165-0270(96)00080-5 
| title = Fractal methods and results in cellular morphology — dimensions, lacunarity and multifractals 
| journal = Journal of Neuroscience Methods 
| volume = 69 
| issue = 2 
| pages = 123–136 
| year = 1996 
| pmid = 8946315 
| s2cid = 20175299 
| url = https://zenodo.org/record/1259855 
}}</ref><ref name="pmid9964879">{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Plotnick | first1 = R. E. 
| last2 = Gardner | first2 = R. H. 
| last3 = Hargrove | first3 = W. W. 
| last4 = Prestegaard | first4 = K. 
| last5 = Perlmutter | first5 = M. 
| title = Lacunarity analysis: A general technique for the analysis of spatial patterns 
| journal = Physical Review E 
| volume = 53 
| issue = 5 
| pages = 5461–8 
| year = 1996 
| pmid = 9964879 | doi=10.1103/physreve.53.5461
| bibcode = 1996PhRvE..53.5461P}}</ref><ref name="plotnick">{{Cite journal | last1 = Plotnick | first1 = R. E. | last2 = Gardner | first2 = R. H. | last3 = O'Neill | first3 = R. V. | doi = 10.1007/BF00125351 | title = Lacunarity indices as measures of landscape texture | journal = Landscape Ecology | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 201 | year = 1993 | s2cid = 7112365 }}</ref> This is illustrated in Figure 1 showing three fractal patterns. When rotated 90°, the first two fairly homogeneous patterns do not appear to change, but the third more heterogeneous figure does change and has correspondingly higher lacunarity. The earliest reference to the term in geometry is usually attributed to [[Benoit Mandelbrot]], who, in 1983 or perhaps as early as 1977, introduced it as, in essence, an adjunct to [[fractal analysis]].<ref name="mandelbrot">{{cite book|title=The Fractal Geometry of Nature| author-link=Benoit Mandelbrot| first=Benoit |last=Mandelbrot| year=1983|isbn=978-0-7167-1186-5 | title-link=The Fractal Geometry of Nature}}</ref> Lacunarity analysis is now used to characterize patterns in a wide variety of fields and has application in multifractal analysis<ref name="Karperien"/><ref name=pmid-18595800>{{cite journal|last1=Al-Kadi|first1=O.S.|last2=Watson|first2=D.|title=Texture Analysis of Aggressive and non-Aggressive Lung Tumor CE CT Images|url=http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/1919/1/tbme.pdf|journal=IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering|volume=55|issue=7|pages=1822–30|year=2008|pmid=18595800|doi=10.1109/TBME.2008.919735|s2cid=14784161|access-date=2014-04-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140413124458/http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/1919/1/tbme.pdf|archive-date=2014-04-13|url-status=dead}}</ref> in particular (see [[#Applications|Applications]]).

== Measuring lacunarity ==
In many patterns or data sets, lacunarity is not readily perceivable or quantifiable, so computer-aided methods have been developed to calculate it. As a measurable quantity, lacunarity is often denoted in scientific literature by the Greek letters <math>\Lambda</math> or <math>\lambda</math> but there is no single standard and several different methods exist to assess and interpret lacunarity.

=== Box counting lacunarity ===
[[File:Fixedstack.gif|thumb|right|400px|Figure 2a. Boxes laid over an image as a fixed grid.
[[File:Slidestack.gif|thumb|right|400px|Figure 2b. Boxes slid over an image in an overlapping pattern.]]]]
One well-known method of determining lacunarity for patterns extracted from digital images uses [[box counting]], the same essential algorithm typically used for some types of [[fractal analysis]].<ref name="smith"/><ref name="mandelbrot"/> Similar to looking at a slide through a microscope with changing levels of magnification, box counting algorithms look at a digital image from many levels of resolution to examine how certain features change with the size of the element used to inspect the image. Basically, the arrangement of pixels is measured using traditionally square (i.e., box-shaped) elements from an arbitrary set of <math>\Epsilon</math> sizes, conventionally denoted <math>\varepsilon</math>s. For each <math>\varepsilon</math>, a box of size <math>\varepsilon</math> is placed successively on the image, in the end covering it completely, and each time it is [[Keel laying|laid down]], the number of pixels that fall within the box is recorded.<ref group="note">This contrasts with [[box counting]] fractal analysis where the ''total number of boxes that contained any pixels'' is counted to determine a fractal dimension.</ref> In '''standard box counting''', the box for each <math>\varepsilon</math> in <math>\Epsilon</math> is placed as though it were part of a grid overlaid on the image so that the box does not overlap itself, but in '''sliding box algorithms''' the box is slid over the image so that it overlaps itself and the "Sliding Box Lacunarity" or SLac is calculated.<ref name="plotnick"/><ref name="wiens"/> Figure 2 illustrates both types of box counting.

==== Calculations from box counting ====
The data gathered for each <math>\varepsilon</math> are manipulated to calculate lacunarity. One measure, denoted here as <math>\lambda_\varepsilon</math>, is found from the [[coefficient of variation]] (<math>\mathit{CV}</math>), calculated as the standard deviation (<math>\sigma</math>) divided by the mean (<math>\mu</math>), for pixels per box.<ref name="smith"/><ref name="plotnick"/><ref name=pmid-18595800/> Because the way an image is sampled will depend on the arbitrary starting location, for any image sampled at any <math>\varepsilon</math> there will be some number (<math>\mathit{G}</math>) of possible orientations, each denoted here by <math>\mathit{g}</math>, that the data can be gathered over, which can have varying effects on the measured distribution of pixels.<ref name="Karperien">{{cite book|title=Defining Microglial Morphology: Form, Function, and Fractal Dimension|author=Karperien|year=2004|publisher=Charles Sturt University|chapter=Chapter 8 Multifractality and Lacunarity|chapter-url=http://bilby.unilinc.edu.au/R/-?func=dbin-jump-full&object_id=31797&silo_library=GEN01|archive-date=2016-03-03|access-date=2025-07-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303221254/http://bilby.unilinc.edu.au/R/-?func=dbin-jump-full&object_id=31797&silo_library=GEN01|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref group="note">See {{harvnb|FracLac|loc=[https://imagej.net/ij/plugins/fraclac/FLHelp/BoxCounting.htm Box Counting]}} for an explanation of methods to address variation with grid location</ref> Equation {{EquationNote|1}} shows the basic method of calculating <math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math>:
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g} = (CV_{\varepsilon,g})^2 = \left( \frac  {\sigma_{\varepsilon,g}}   {\mu_{\varepsilon,g}}  \right)^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

===== Probability distributions =====
Alternatively, some methods sort the numbers of pixels counted into a probability distribution having <math>B</math> bins, and use the bin sizes (masses, <math>m</math>) and their corresponding probabilities (<math>p</math>) to calculate <math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math> according to Equations {{EquationNote|2}} through {{EquationNote|5}}: 
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\mu_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{B} {m_{i,\varepsilon} p_{i,\varepsilon}}</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\mathit{v}_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{B} {\left( m_{i,\varepsilon} - \mu_{\varepsilon} \right ) ^2 p_{i,\varepsilon}}</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2=\mathit{v}_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{B} {m_{i,\varepsilon}^2 p_{i,\varepsilon}-\mu_{\varepsilon}^2}</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\lambda_{\varepsilon}= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{B} {m_{i,\varepsilon}^2 p_{i,\varepsilon}-\mu_{\varepsilon}^2}}{\mu_{\varepsilon}^2} = \frac{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2}{\mu_{\varepsilon}^2}</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}

==== Interpreting ''&lambda;'' ====
Lacunarity based on <math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math> has been assessed in several ways including by using the variation in or the average value of <math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math> for each <math>\varepsilon</math> (see Equation {{EquationNote|6}}) and by using the variation in or average over all grids (see Equation {{EquationNote|7}}).<ref name="smith"/><ref name="Karperien"/><ref name="wiens">{{Cite journal | last1 = McIntyre | first1 = N. E. | last2 = Wiens | first2 = J. A. | journal = Landscape Ecology | volume = 15 |title=A novel use of the lacunarity index to discern landscape function| issue = 4 | pages = 313 | year = 2000 | doi = 10.1023/A:1008148514268 | s2cid = 18644861 }}</ref><ref name="Jelinek"/>
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\overline{\lambda_{g}}=\frac{\sum_{\varepsilon=1}^\Epsilon \lambda_{\varepsilon,g}}{\Epsilon}</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\Lambda = \frac{\sum_{\mathit{g}=1}^\mathit{G} \overline{\lambda_{g}}}{\mathit{G}}</math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}

===== Relationship to the fractal dimension =====
Lacunarity analyses using the types of values discussed above have shown that data sets extracted from dense fractals, from patterns that change little when rotated, or from patterns that are homogeneous, have low lacunarity, but as these features increase,{{clarify|What increases lacunarity, repetition of low-lac. pattern, or another feature?|date=October 2012}} so generally does lacunarity. In some instances, it has been demonstrated that fractal dimensions and values of lacunarity were correlated,<ref name="smith"/> but more recent research has shown that this relationship does not hold for all types of patterns and measures of lacunarity.<ref name="Karperien"/> Indeed, as Mandelbrot originally proposed, lacunarity has been shown to be useful in discerning amongst patterns (e.g., fractals, textures, etc.) that share or have similar [[fractal dimension]]s in a variety of scientific fields including neuroscience.<ref name="Jelinek">{{cite book|title=8th European Conference on Mathematical and Theoretical Biology, Kraków |first1=Herbert |last1=Jelinek |first2=Audrey |last2=Karperien |first3=Nebojsa |last3=Milosevic |chapter= Lacunarity Analysis and Classification of Microglia in Neuroscience|date=June 2011|chapter-url=http://www.impan.pl/~ecmtb11/showabstract.php?id=Jelinek_Herbert1}}</ref>

==== Graphical lacunarity ====
Other methods of assessing lacunarity from box counting data use the relationship between values of lacunarity (e.g., <math>\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math>) and <math>\varepsilon</math> in different ways from the ones noted above. One such method looks at the <math>\ln</math> vs <math>\ln</math> plot of these values. According to this method, the curve itself can be analyzed visually, or the slope at <math>\mathit{g}</math> can be calculated from the <math>\ln</math> vs <math>\ln</math> regression line.<ref name="plotnick"/><ref name="wiens"/> Because they tend to behave in certain ways for respectively mono-, multi-, and non-fractal patterns, <math>\ln</math> vs <math>\ln</math> lacunarity plots have been used to supplement methods of classifying such patterns.<ref name="Karperien"/><ref name="Jelinek"/>

To make the plots for this type of analysis, the data from box counting first have to be transformed as in Equation {{EquationNote|9}}:
{{NumBlk|:|<math>f \lambda_{\varepsilon,g}=\lambda_{\varepsilon,g}+1</math>|{{EquationRef|9}}}}
This transformation avoids undefined values, which is important because homogeneous images will have <math>\sigma</math> at some <math>\varepsilon</math> equal to 0 so that the slope of the <math>\ln</math> vs <math>\ln</math> regression line would be impossible to find. With <math>f \lambda_{\varepsilon,g}</math>, homogeneous images have a slope of 0, corresponding intuitively to the idea of no rotational or translational invariance and no gaps.<ref>{{cite web|author=Karperien|title=Interpreting Lacunarity |year=2002 |work=FracLac |url=http://rsb.info.nih.gov/ij/plugins/fraclac/FLHelp/lactutorial.htm#oneplus|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080920054010/http://rsb.info.nih.gov/ij/plugins/fraclac/FLHelp/lactutorial.htm#oneplus|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 20, 2008}}</ref>

One box counting technique using a "gliding" box calculates lacunarity according to: 
{{NumBlk|:| <math>
\mathcal{L}(r) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{r^2} S_i^2 Q(S_i,r)}{ \left( \sum_{i=1}^{r^2}  S_i Q(S_i,r) \right)^2 }.</math>|{{EquationRef|10}}}}
<math>S_i</math> is the number of filled data points in the box and <math>Q(S_i,r)</math> the normalized [[Frequency (statistics)|frequency distribution]] of <math>S_i</math> for different box sizes.

==== Prefactor lacunarity ====
Another proposed way of assessing lacunarity using box counting, the ''Prefactor'' method, is based on the value obtained from box counting for the fractal dimension (<math>D_B</math>). This statistic uses the variable <math>A</math> from the scaling rule <math>N = A \varepsilon^{-D_B}</math>, where <math>A</math> is calculated from the y-intercept (<math>\mathit{y}</math>) of the ln-ln regression line for <math>\varepsilon</math> and either the count (<math>N</math>) of boxes that had any pixels at all in them or else <math>m</math> at <math>g</math>. <math>A</math> is particularly affected by image size and the way data are gathered, especially by the lower limit of <math>\varepsilon</math>s used. The final measure is calculated as shown in Equations {{EquationNote|11}} through {{EquationNote|13}}:<ref name="smith"/><ref name="mandelbrot"/>
{{NumBlk|:|<math>A_g = \frac{1}{e^{\mathit{y}_g}}</math>|{{EquationRef|11}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>\overline{A} = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^G A_g}{G} </math>|{{EquationRef|12}}}}
{{NumBlk|:|<math>P \Lambda = \frac {  \sum_{g=1}^G { \left ( {\frac{A_g}{\overline A}}-1   \right ) ^2}}{G} </math>|{{EquationRef|13}}}}
